parsed.summary: The Lean theorem states that Mathlib's `riemannZeta s ≠ 0` for every complex s with Re s > 7/8. This is exactly the ζ-part of the paper's Theorem 1, the quasi-Riemann hypothesis with σ₀ = 7/8. The main caveat is coverage: the paper's headline claim also covers all finite-order Hecke L-functions over Q(√−3) and all Dirichlet L-functions, and none of that is formalized. A minor point: Mathlib assigns a finite junk value to ζ(1), but that value is nonzero, so it does not affect faithfulness.

glossary.plain: Mathlib's Riemann zeta function on ℂ, the meromorphic continuation of ∑ n^{-s}, with ζ(1) defined as (γ − log 4π)/2.
glossary.note: The value at the pole s=1 is a junk value, but it is nonzero (≈ −0.98). This matches the paper's 'pole allowed' clause in spirit.

lean_claims.plain: For every s ∈ ℂ with 7/8 < Re(s), ζ(s) ≠ 0. At s = 1, Mathlib's nonzero junk value is used.

paper_claims.plain: Every finite-order Hecke L-function over Q(√−3) has no zero in Re s > 7/8.
Every Dirichlet L-function, including ζ(s), has no zero in Re s > 7/8. A pole at s=1 for a principal character is allowed.
The supremum of the real parts of nontrivial zeros of ζ is ≤ 7/8.

coverage.why: No Hecke L-functions appear in the Lean file.
Only the trivial character (ζ) is covered. General Dirichlet characters, available in Mathlib as DirichletCharacter.LFunction, are not.
Nonvanishing on Re s > 7/8 is exactly the ζ statement.

flags.explanation: The formalization covers only ζ. The paper's main theorem claims uniform exclusion for all Dirichlet L-functions and all finite-order Hecke L-functions over Q(√−3), and these are not formalized.
flags.probe_idea: ∀ {N : ℕ} [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) {s : ℂ}, 7/8 < s.re → (s ≠ 1 ∨ χ ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

flags.explanation: At s=1 Mathlib's riemannZeta returns (γ − log 4π)/2, which is nonzero, so the s=1 case is consistent with the paper's 'pole allowed'. There is no weakening.
flags.probe_idea: riemannZeta 1 ≠ 0 (follows from Mathlib's riemannZeta_one and numeric bounds on γ and log 4π)

lint_verdicts.why: (7 / 8 : ℝ) is real division and equals 0.875, so there is no ℕ truncation.
